review-neurips-2026-150736.title: Soft-Radial Projection for Constrained End-to-End Learning

checks.claim: Absolute continuity of the data implies a continuously differentiable L-smooth expected objective.
checks.explanation: An absolutely continuous input law can be collapsed onto a kink by the network. Even without collapse, an unbounded input density near a projection kink can prevent a Lipschitz gradient after averaging.
checks.demonstration:
Use \(C=[-1,1]\), anchor zero, and the admissible radial function

\[
r(\rho)=\frac12+\frac{\rho}{2(1+\rho)}.
\]

For an input law uniform on \([0,1]\), let the network ignore the input: \(g_\theta(Z)=\max(\theta,0)\). With smooth loss \(\ell(x)=x\),

\[
F(\theta)=p(\max(\theta,0)),\qquad F'_{-}(0)=0,\qquad F'_{+}(0)=\frac12.
\]

Thus an absolutely continuous input can still give a nondifferentiable expected objective.

A separate example avoids collapse: let \(g_\theta(z)=z+\theta\) and choose the normalized density

\[
f(z)=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{|z-1|}},\qquad 0<|z-1|<\frac14.
\]

The output has no boundary atom. At \(u=1\), the projection derivative drops from \(1\) to \(1/4\). The mass crossing that kink as \(h\downarrow0\) gives

\[
F^{\prime}(h)-F^{\prime}(0)=-\frac34\sqrt h+O(h).
\]

The averaged derivative is continuous but not Lipschitz near zero. Smooth-piece derivative bounds and absence of boundary atoms therefore do not establish the claimed smooth regime.
checks.repair: A sufficient smooth regime requires differentiable sample composites, a dominated gradient, and an integrable common gradient-Lipschitz bound on a neighborhood of the parameter set. Uniformly controlled smooth components whose projected images stay a positive distance from all kinks are a concrete sufficient case. The SGD rate also requires an unbiased oracle with bounded variance and a lower objective bound. Absolute continuity of the inputs alone supplies none of these gradient bounds.
checks.scope: Both examples meet the radial assumptions. The second also avoids boundary atoms and respects smooth-piece derivative bounds, so excluding distribution collapse alone is insufficient.
checks.title: Absolutely continuous data do not ensure a smooth expected objective
checks.claimFormula: \mathbb P_Z\ll\lambda\quad\Longrightarrow\quad F\in C^1(K),\qquad\|\nabla F(\theta)-\nabla F(\theta^{\prime})\|\leq L\|\theta-\theta^{\prime}\|\quad(\theta,\theta^{\prime}\in K)
checks.whyItMatters: The claimed \(O(T^{-1/2})\) smooth-SGD rate cannot be justified by input absolute continuity alone.
checks.claimContext: Proposition 3.5(1) considers \(F(\theta)=\mathbb E_Z[\ell(p(g_\theta(Z)))]\), with compact parameter iterates. It infers continuous differentiability and a Lipschitz gradient from absolute continuity of the input law with respect to Lebesgue measure.

checks.location: Proposition3.5(2), displayed convergence of Clarke subgradient norm; AppendixB.2
checks.claim: Stochastic subgradient descent has expected minimum Clarke subgradient norm tending to zero.
checks.explanation: The cited tame-function theorem gives stationary cluster points, not continuity of the subgradient residual along the approaching iterates. The displayed limit fails even for a bounded noiseless convex example.
checks.demonstration:
The convex tame objective \(F(\theta)=|\theta|\) can be realized within the architecture. Take \(C=\mathbb R\) and

\[
r(\rho)=\frac{1+\rho}{2+\rho},\qquad p(u)=u\,r(u^2),\qquad g_\theta(z)=\theta,\qquad\ell(x)=|p^{-1}(x)|.
\]

The inverse is locally Lipschitz and semialgebraic. Start at \(\theta_0=\sqrt2/10\) and use exact noiseless subgradients with \(\eta_t=1/(t+2)\):

\[
\theta_{t+1}=\theta_t-\frac{\operatorname{sign}(\theta_t)}{t+2}.
\]

Every iterate is the irrational initial value minus a rational number, so it never equals zero. Consequently

\[
\partial_C F(\theta_t)=\{\operatorname{sign}(\theta_t)\},\qquad\min_{v\in\partial_C F(\theta_t)}\|v\|=1
\]

at every finite step. The steps are nonsummable and square summable. The iterates stay bounded and converge to zero: a fixed eventual sign would contradict the divergent sum of steps, while every sign-crossing overshoot is at most the vanishing step. Thus all cluster points are stationary even though the displayed expected Clarke-norm limit fails.
checks.repair: Use the actual Davis theorem: under its bounded-iterate, step, martingale-noise, moment and chain-rule/tameness hypotheses, every cluster point is Clarke stationary and objective values converge. With compact iterates this also gives \(\operatorname{dist}(\theta_t,\operatorname{Crit}F)\to0\), and expected distance tends to zero by bounded convergence. This is a distance to the stationary set, not \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial_C F(\theta_t))\). Additional continuity/regularity would be needed to retain the latter limit.
checks.scope: The counterexample satisfies the stronger appendix step assumptions and has zero noise. It agrees with, rather than contradicts, the cited stationary-limit-point theorem.
checks.title: Stationary limit points do not imply vanishing Clarke norms at iterates
checks.whyItMatters: An iterate can approach a stationary point while this subgradient norm stays equal to one.
checks.claimContext: Proposition 3.5(2) and Appendix B.2 strengthen stochastic subgradient convergence to a zero expected minimum Clarke-subgradient norm at the current iterate.
